reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Also termed myosin storage myopathy, caused by variants in MYH7 encoding slow/beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain, usually with autosomal dominant inheritance
Weakness may be predominantly proximal (scapuloperoneal or limb-girdle) or distal, with considerable phenotypic variability even within families
Because MYH7 also causes cardiomyopathy, associated hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy can occur and mandates cardiac assessment
Onset ranges from childhood to adulthood with generally slow progression
The muscle biopsy hallmark is subsarcolemmal hyaline bodies within type 1 fibres, which stain for myosin and are pale on routine oxidative enzyme stains
Creatine kinase is normal or mildly elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern
The hyaline bodies represent accumulation of the mutant myosin, distinguishing the entity on histochemistry and electron microscopy
Diagnosis combines the histological finding of hyaline bodies with MYH7 genetic confirmation and cardiac evaluation
reference.pathophysiology: Hyaline body (myosin storage) myopathy is caused by dominant variants in MYH7, encoding the slow/beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain expressed in type 1 skeletal fibres and the heart. The mutations, often clustered in the distal rod domain of the protein, impair proper folding and assembly of the myosin thick filament, causing the abnormal myosin to accumulate as subsarcolemmal hyaline inclusions. Disruption of the contractile apparatus in slow-twitch fibres produces skeletal muscle weakness, and because the same protein is essential in cardiac muscle, patients are at risk of an associated cardiomyopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Laing distal myopathy and other MYH7-related phenotypes
Scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy of other cause
Congenital myopathies including core and rod myopathies
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with histochemistry, immunostaining for myosin, and electron microscopy to demonstrate hyaline bodies
Muscle MRI to define the distribution of involvement
Cardiac evaluation with ECG and echocardiography
Targeted MYH7 sequencing or a congenital myopathy/distal myopathy panel
redFlags: Symptoms or signs of hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy
Arrhythmia or syncope in the patient or affected relatives
Respiratory muscle weakness with reduced vital capacity
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Skeletal muscle weakness generally progresses slowly and many patients remain ambulant, but the overall prognosis is strongly influenced by any associated MYH7 cardiomyopathy, so cardiac surveillance is a key determinant of outcome.
pitfalls: Neglecting cardiac screening despite the well-recognised MYH7 cardiac association
Confusing hyaline bodies with other inclusions such as cytoplasmic or reducing bodies without appropriate stains
Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes a myopathy
Missing the diagnosis when weakness is proximal and mistaken for limb-girdle dystrophy
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-specific drug therapy exists, so care centres on physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve strength and mobility and prevent contractures

Regular cardiac surveillance with ECG and echocardiography, treating any associated hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy with heart-failure and antiarrhythmic therapy and considering an implantable defibrillator where indicated
Respiratory monitoring for respiratory muscle weakness with non-invasive ventilatory support once hypoventilation develops
Orthopaedic management of contractures and spinal deformity with orthoses, stretching, and mobility aids
Careful anaesthetic assessment given the cardiac and respiratory involvement
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular care including neurology, cardiology, and respiratory medicine
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with cascade cardiac and clinical screening of at-risk relatives
